title: Glasshouse and Interior
premise: Casper Sterling, a piano tuner who has spent decades listening to buildings rather than people, is hired to tune the piano in the house of Mirela Voss, the last fluent speaker of Vessic, a dying language from a drowned river valley. She asks him to become her final student, and as he learns, he realizes she is not teaching him words but asking him to carry an untranslatable sentence—one that names what was lost when her village was flooded—into the world after she dies. When developers announce the rerouting of the last bus line to the old neighborhood, Casper must choose between his perfected invisibility and speaking the sentence aloud at the city's transit hearing. He translates it, testifies in imperfect Vessic, and ends the novel not fluent or healed, but finally audible—keeping the language alive by living with what it says.
about_author: Xanthe Montrose is the pen name of a former architectural conservator who spent years cataloguing condemned buildings before their demolition. Their fiction explores how places hold people and how people fail to hold each other.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: POV Casper. We meet Casper mid-job, tuning a piano in an empty office lobby, narrating how he reads rooms through resonance and uses his practiced smile to end conversations before they begin. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as competence.

chapters.title: A House That Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Casper. A referral sends him to a sagging Victorian on Delmore Street, where the radiators clank out what he swears is grief. The owner, Mirela Voss, watches him work without speaking, then asks if he can hear what the house is saying. Beat: recognition between two listeners.

chapters.title: One Final Student
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Mirela reveals she is the last speaker of Vessic and offers to teach him—not for money, but because 'a language needs two mouths.' He declines, then returns that night, unable to explain why. Beat: the first crack in his invisibility.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: POV Casper. First lessons: water words, door words, apology words. Casper learns Vessic has no word for 'stranger,' only 'not-yet-kin.' His smile fails for the first time when Mirela catches him practicing alone. Beat: tentative belonging.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Said
chapters.summary: POV Mirela. Her chapter: the flooded valley of Ves, the 1958 dam, the village that exists now only in her mouth. She chose Casper because he already listens to houses. Beat: grief given structure.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Flashbacks to his father's silence and the childhood stutter he buried under the smile. A client tries to make small talk; he deflects, then realizes he told Mirela things he's never told anyone. Beat: fear of being known.

chapters.title: Grammar of Absence
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Lessons deepen: Vessic verbs conjugate for memory—things seen, things told, things forgotten. Casper struggles with the 'forgotten' form until Mirela says he's been conjugating his whole life in it. Beat: language as mirror.

chapters.title: The Rerouting Notice
chapters.summary: POV Casper. A notice taped to the bus shelter: the 47 line to the old neighborhood will be rerouted in three months. Mirela reads it aloud twice, once in English, once in Vessic, and the second version makes Casper weep without knowing why. Beat: encroaching loss.

chapters.title: Not-Yet-Kin
chapters.summary: POV Mirela. She visits Casper's apartment, the first guest in nine years, and quietly catalogs his life: the metronome, the unsent letters, the photo of a mother he never mentions. Beat: being witnessed against one's will.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Mirela teaches him a single sentence she refuses to translate: 'Shal velessa koru im.' She says he must live with it before she'll give its meaning. He repeats it like a tune he can't place. Beat: mystery as invitation.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: POV Casper. His tuning work suffers—he hears Vessic cadences inside clients' pianos. A wealthy client complains; he loses the account. His sister calls after years of silence; he lets it ring. Beat: the old self decaying.

chapters.title: Mirela's Hospital Winter
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Mirela is hospitalized; lessons move to a ward room where nurses mistake Vessic for singing. Casper begins recording her voice, telling himself it's for study. Beat: urgency beneath denial.

chapters.title: Things Told, Things Forgotten
chapters.summary: POV Mirela. From her bed, she tells the story of her brother, who took the last boat off the dam site and never wrote back—the sentence, she hints, belongs to him. Beat: the wound beneath the language.

chapters.title: The Archive People
chapters.summary: POV Casper. University linguists arrive with recording equipment, treating Mirela as data. Casper, protective, argues with a young researcher who insists languages outlive speakers. Beat: anger on behalf of the voiceless.

chapters.title: Discharged
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Mirela insists on going home to die in the house. Casper moves in temporarily as caretaker, sleeping in the flooded-valley boyhood room she kept intact. Beat: intimacy through duty.

chapters.title: Translation Attempt
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Alone in the house, Casper attempts the sentence's meaning and gets it wrong three times—'I miss you,' 'I am sorry,' 'come home'—each failure revealing more of himself than of Vessic. Beat: humility.

chapters.title: The Last Bus
chapters.summary: POV Casper. He rides the 47 line end to end the night before rerouting, recording radiator-song and window-rattle, realizing the bus itself is a sentence about to be deleted. Beat: elegy in motion.

chapters.title: Shal Velessa Koru Im
chapters.summary: POV Mirela. On her final lucid night, she gives the translation: 'The water remembers our names even though we cannot say them back.' It is both lament and instruction. Beat: transmission complete.

chapters.title: Silence in the House
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Mirela dies on a Tuesday. Casper tunes her silent piano, finds her lesson notebooks, and discovers she'd written his name in Vessic on the last page—as kin. Beat: grief with a task inside it.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: POV Casper. At the transit hearing, Casper abandons his prepared statement and speaks the sentence aloud in Vessic, then translates it, voice shaking, stutter resurfacing—and keeps talking anyway. Beat: climax; invisibility abandoned.

chapters.title: Two Mouths
chapters.summary: POV Casper. Weeks later: the young linguist asks Casper to co-teach a community class; his sister visits; the bus route is rerouted but a memorial plaque carries Mirela's sentence. Beat: belonging chosen, not granted.

chapters.title: The Water Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Casper. At the reservoir above the drowned valley, Casper teaches his first student—a ten-year-old from the old neighborhood—the water words. He no longer needs the smile. Beat: resolution; the language lives in a second mouth.
